opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction for me comes down to where the motivation starts. If impact itself is the goal, you end up chasing whatever looks big at the moment: the hottest topic, the most citations, the flashiest demo. You can be very busy and very visible and still not change much, because you're optimizing for the appearance of mattering rather than for a specific problem getting solved.

The impact I care about starts from a concrete problem I believe needs to be solved. In my own work on systems for large language models, I asked a pretty plain question: why is it so expensive and slow to actually run these models, and what's stopping more people from using them? If we can make serving faster and cheaper, and make the tools open so anyone can build on them, that changes what researchers, startups, and students can do. The impact is a consequence of solving the problem well, not something I aim at directly.

One test I use is to ask myself: if nobody ever knew this was my work, would I still want it to exist? If yes, I'm probably working on something I actually care about. If the main appeal is the recognition, that's a warning sign.

Another is whether real people are using it and whether it makes their lives easier. Open source keeps me honest that way. People adopt your project because it solves their problem, not because of your title or a paper award. When users file issues, contribute back, or build things you never imagined, that's the kind of impact that feels real to me.

So I'd say impact is a good compass but a bad destination. Use it to choose problems worth your time, and then focus on doing the work well. The impact follows from that.

r001.rationale: It contrasts chasing impact or visibility as the goal with starting from a concrete problem she wants solved, and treats impact as a consequence of that work.

r002.rationale: The response says she would want the work to exist even if nobody knew it was hers. It does not say she wants the change realized regardless of whether she personally brings it about.

r003.rationale: It recommends focusing on doing the work well, but does not state that sustained pursuit of what one truly wants depends on one’s own persistence.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because I think the two can look identical from the outside and feel completely different from the inside.

When I say I care about impact, what I mean is pretty concrete. I want the thing I build to actually be used by people, and I want it to change what they can do. With SGLang, for example, the impact I care about is that someone with a few GPUs can serve a model faster and cheaper than they could before, and that a researcher can try an idea in an afternoon instead of a week. Those are things I can point to. There's a user, there's a before and after, and I can check whether it's real.

Making impact as a goal in itself is different. It's when the metric becomes the target. You start asking "how do I get more stars, more citations, more people saying my name," and the work bends toward whatever produces those signals. The trouble is that those signals are noisy. You can get a lot of attention for something that doesn't actually help anyone, and you can do something genuinely useful that nobody notices for a year. If you optimize for the signal, you end up chasing hype cycles and you lose the ability to tell whether you're doing good work.

So the test I use on myself is something like: if nobody ever knew I did this, would I still think it was worth doing? For the work I'm proudest of, the answer is yes. The open source community figured out a lot of what we did before we wrote anything down, and that was fine, because the point was that the system worked.

I'll also admit it's not a clean separation. Visibility does matter, because a project nobody knows about doesn't get adopted, and adoption is where the real impact comes from. So I don't think ambition is the problem. The problem is when ambition detaches from the actual user and starts running on its own. I try to keep the user in the loop as the thing I'm accountable to, and let the recognition be a side effect rather than the plan.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts concrete changes for users—such as faster, cheaper model serving—with pursuing recognition signals like stars and citations for their own sake.

r002.rationale: It says the work is worthwhile even if nobody knows Ying did it, but does not state that she values the desired impact regardless of whether she personally brings it about.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that sustained pursuit of what one wants to accomplish depends on personal persistence.

astra-6.text:
For me, the distinction is whether I care about the actual outcome or just the idea that I’ve done something impactful. “Impact” on its own is pretty vague. You have to ask: impact on whom, and in what way? Something can affect a lot of people without making their lives better.

So I’d start with a problem I think is worth solving, then ask whether my work actually helps. A useful check is: if nobody knew I was involved, would I still want this to happen? If the answer is yes, that’s closer to the impact I care about. Scale can matter, but it comes after deciding what’s worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts valuing an actual outcome and whether it helps with pursuing the vague idea of having made an impact.

r002.rationale: The hypothetical asks whether she would still want the outcome if nobody knew she was involved. It addresses recognition, but does not clearly say she wants it realized regardless of whether she personally brings it about.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss persistence or sustained pursuit depending on one’s own persistence.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the distinction is between caring about a particular outcome and caring about being the person who makes something big happen. Those can look similar from the outside, but they lead to different decisions.

If I care about a problem, then learning that someone else has solved it is good news. I might help them, or move on to another problem. If what I really want is to have impact myself, I might feel disappointed—even though the outcome I said I wanted has happened.

So I try to ask: What do I actually want to be different, and for whom? Would I still want that outcome if I got no credit for it? That helps me keep impact connected to something concrete, rather than treating scale or recognition as the goal.

r001.rationale: It contrasts wanting a particular problem solved with wanting to be the person who makes a big impact.

r002.rationale: It says someone else solving the problem would be good news and asks whether she would still want the outcome without personal credit.

r003.rationale: It does not state that accomplishing what one truly wants ultimately depends on one’s own persistence.
